categories.label: Behavior Definition
categories.description: Turning a program goal or vague intent into a defined, measurable target.

categories.label: Diagnosis
categories.description: Explaining why a defined behavior isn't happening (barriers, drivers, root causes).

categories.label: Intervention Design
categories.description: Turning a diagnosis into candidate levers, messages, or intervention content.

categories.label: Measurement
categories.description: Choosing, adapting, or building instruments to measure a behavior or construct.

categories.label: Research Methods
categories.description: Analytical or methodological operations (e.g. effect size adjustment, model specification).

categories.label: Segmentation & Personas
categories.description: Grouping people or contexts into behaviorally meaningful segments.

categories.label: Risk & Pre-Mortem
categories.description: Anticipating backfire effects, failure points, or unintended consequences before launch.

categories.label: Cultural Context
categories.description: Assessing how a cultural or contextual lens changes what will work.

stages.label: Define
stages.description: Establishing what behavior, population, or outcome the work is about.

stages.label: Diagnose
stages.description: Understanding why the current behavior pattern exists.

stages.label: Test
stages.description: Planning or analyzing an evaluation of an intervention.

io_types.label: Program goal statement
io_types.description: A practitioner's plain-language description of what a program is trying to achieve, plus whatever context they have on the target population and setting. Typically vague and not yet a measurable behavior.

io_types.label: Target behavior brief
io_types.description: One measurable, observable target behavior specified as who + what + when, plus a prioritized list of runner-up candidate behaviors with the reasoning for why the top choice won.

io_types.label: COM-B barrier hypotheses
io_types.description: Competing Capability / Opportunity / Motivation barrier hypotheses for one target behavior, each with the diagnostic question(s) that would discriminate it from the others.

skills.name: comb-barrier-decomposer
skills.title: COM-B Barrier Decomposer
skills.description: Use when one specific, already-defined target behavior exists (a clear who + what + when, not a goal or outcome) and the question on the table is "why isn't this happening yet?" Invoke immediately after key-behavior-definer, or any time a defined behavior is handed over without an accompanying barrier diagnosis. Do not invoke on a vague program goal — that has to become one defined behavior first, or the barriers produced here will be diagnosing the wrong thing.

evidence_base.citation: Michie, S., van Stralen, M. M., & West, R. (2011). The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions. Implementation Science, 6(42).
Michie, S., Atkins, L., & West, R. (2014). The Behaviour Change Wheel: A Guide to Designing Interventions. Silverback Publishing, Ch. 2.

weird_context.note: COM-B is presented as a universal model of behavior (its three components are meant to be exhaustive by construction, not culturally contingent), but the diagnostic question bank and worked examples in the source literature skew toward UK health-behavior contexts. The Opportunity (social) sub-component in particular tends to need the most local adaptation — what counts as socially sanctioned or normal varies more than the framework's examples suggest.

inputs.description: The single defined target behavior (who + what + when) to diagnose. Normally the output of key-behavior-definer, but any equivalently specific behavior statement works.

outputs.description: Competing Capability / Opportunity / Motivation barrier hypotheses for the target behavior, each paired with the diagnostic question(s) that would discriminate it from the others.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.markdown:
Decomposes one defined target behavior into competing Capability,
Opportunity, and Motivation barrier hypotheses, each attached to the
diagnostic question that would tell you whether that specific hypothesis is
the one actually holding the behavior back.

sections.heading: When to invoke it
sections.markdown:
- A target behavior brief exists (who + what + when) and the next question
  is "why isn't this happening already?"
- A team is about to jump straight to intervention ideas ("let's send a
  reminder text") without having named a barrier the intervention is meant
  to address.
- Multiple plausible explanations for non-behavior are being asserted
  informally ("maybe they forgot", "maybe it's too expensive", "maybe
  they don't think it matters") and need to be organized into testable,
  mutually exclusive hypotheses.
- Do **not** invoke on a goal or outcome statement — route it through
  [key-behavior-definer](../key-behavior-definer) first. A barrier
  decomposition of "improve maternal health" has nothing concrete to
  attach to.

sections.heading: What it draws on
sections.markdown:
The COM-B model: behavior (B) occurs when a person has sufficient
**C**apability (psychological — knowledge, skills, ability to self-regulate;
physical — strength, stamina, dexterity), **O**pportunity (physical — time,
resources, location; social — norms, sanction, support from others), and
**M**otivation (reflective — beliefs, intentions, evaluations; automatic —
habit, emotion, impulse) at the moment the behavior needs to occur. Because
the three components are constructed to be jointly exhaustive, a rigorous
decomposition should be able to state at least one hypothesis per
sub-component even if some are quickly ruled out — the discipline is in
naming what would distinguish a real barrier from a plausible-sounding one,
not in generating the longest list.

sections.heading: Output template
sections.markdown:
```markdown
# COM-B Barrier Hypotheses

**Target behavior:** <who + what + when, carried over verbatim>

sections.heading: Capability
sections.markdown:
### Physical
- **Hypothesis:** <specific barrier — e.g. "lacks the physical skill to complete the form unassisted">
  **Diagnostic question:** <question whose answer would confirm/rule this out>
### Psychological
- **Hypothesis:** <e.g. "doesn't know the deadline exists">
  **Diagnostic question:** <...>

sections.heading: Opportunity
sections.markdown:
### Physical
- **Hypothesis:** <e.g. "the clinic is only open during work hours">
  **Diagnostic question:** <...>
### Social
- **Hypothesis:** <e.g. "attending would signal something the person wants to avoid signaling">
  **Diagnostic question:** <...>

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.markdown:
### Reflective
- **Hypothesis:** <e.g. "doesn't believe the behavior will produce the promised benefit">
  **Diagnostic question:** <...>
### Automatic
- **Hypothesis:** <e.g. "competing habitual behavior crowds out the window to act">
  **Diagnostic question:** <...>

sections.heading: Most likely barrier(s), pending diagnostic answers
sections.markdown:
<1-3 sentences ranking which hypotheses seem most probable given whatever
context is available, flagged clearly as provisional until the diagnostic
questions are actually answered in the field>
```

sections.heading: Known failure modes
sections.markdown:
- **Motivation as a dumping ground.** It's easy to label every unexplained
  non-behavior "lack of motivation" because it requires no further
  evidence. If a hypothesis can't be stated specifically enough to produce
  a diagnostic question that could rule it *out*, it isn't a real
  hypothesis yet.
- **Capability/Opportunity confusion.** "Doesn't know how" (capability) and
  "was never told" (opportunity, if the information was never made
  available to them) get mislabeled constantly. The distinguishing test is
  whether the barrier would persist even if the environment fully
  supported the person — if yes, it's capability; if the environment is
  actually the blocker, it's opportunity.
- **Non-discriminating questions.** A diagnostic question that would get
  the same answer regardless of which hypothesis is true isn't
  discriminating — it's just a survey item. Each question should be
  chosen because a different hypothesis predicts a different answer.
- **Running on a compound or vague behavior.** If the input behavior still
  contains "and" or lacks a clear who/what/when, the barriers produced will
  quietly diagnose whichever half of the behavior was easiest to picture,
  not the behavior as actually specified.
- **Treating the ranked barriers as confirmed.** This skill produces
  hypotheses and the questions to test them, not a diagnosis. Passing the
  "most likely barrier" straight to intervention design without answering
  the diagnostic questions in the field skips the step the questions exist
  for.

skills.name: key-behavior-definer
skills.title: Key Behavior Definer
skills.description: Use when a program goal, campaign objective, or "theory of change" is stated in vague, aspirational, or attitudinal terms (e.g. "increase savings", "improve maternal health", "reduce dropout", "build trust in the vaccine") and no single measurable, observable behavior has been named yet. Invoke before any diagnosis, intervention-design, or measurement skill in this library, since all of them require one defined target behavior as input. Do not invoke once a specific who + what + when behavior is already agreed — that's a sign this step is done.

evidence_base.framework: Behaviour Change Wheel — specifying and selecting target behaviours
evidence_base.citation: Michie, S., Atkins, L., & West, R. (2014). The Behaviour Change Wheel: A Guide to Designing Interventions. Silverback Publishing, Ch. 3.
Michie, S., Atkins, L., & West, R. (2014). The Behaviour Change Wheel: A Guide to Designing Interventions. Silverback Publishing, pp. 46-48.

weird_context.note: The BCW's target-behaviour-selection logic itself is context-agnostic (it's a prioritization procedure, not a claim about what motivates people), but the worked examples and APEASE weighting in the source literature are drawn overwhelmingly from UK/US public health programs. Treat the *procedure* as portable and the *illustrative priors* (e.g. which behaviors are usually "high impact") as needing local validation.

inputs.description: The program or campaign goal as originally stated, plus whatever context is available on the target population, setting, and known constraints (budget, delivery channel, timeline).

outputs.description: One measurable, observable target behavior specified as who + what + when, plus a prioritized list of runner-up candidate behaviors with the reasoning for why the top choice won.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.markdown:
Turns one vague program goal into a single measurable, observable target
behavior — specified as who does what, by when — backed by a prioritized
list of the other candidate behaviors that were considered and set aside.

sections.heading: When to invoke it
sections.markdown:
- A program document, funder brief, or stakeholder states a goal as an
  outcome, attitude, or aspiration rather than a behavior ("increase
  financial resilience", "improve engagement", "reduce stigma").
- Someone asks "what should we actually be trying to change here?" or "what
  behavior are we targeting?"
- Multiple candidate behaviors are floating around informally and the team
  needs one to commit to before diagnosis or design work starts.
- Do **not** invoke if a specific, already-observable behavior with a named
  actor and timeframe is on the table — hand that directly to a diagnosis
  skill (e.g. [comb-barrier-decomposer](../comb-barrier-decomposer)) instead.

sections.heading: What it draws on
sections.markdown:
The Behaviour Change Wheel's "select target behaviour" step: generate a
reasonably exhaustive list of candidate behaviors that could plausibly
achieve the stated goal, then score each against the APEASE criteria —
**A**ffordability, **P**racticability, **E**ffectiveness (and cost-
effectiveness), **A**cceptability, **S**ide-effects/safety, **E**quity —
plus impact (how much changing this behavior would move the goal) and
spillover (whether changing it makes other useful behaviors more or less
likely). The highest-scoring candidate becomes the target; the rest are
kept as a ranked shortlist rather than discarded, since diagnosis on the
top choice sometimes fails and a team needs a documented next option.

sections.heading: Output template
sections.markdown:
```markdown
# Target Behavior Brief

**Program goal (as given):** <verbatim or lightly cleaned goal statement>

sections.heading: Selected target behavior
sections.markdown:
- **Who:** <actor — e.g. "first-time mothers in program clinics">
- **What:** <single observable action — e.g. "attend the 6-week postnatal check">
- **When:** <window — e.g. "within 6-8 weeks of delivery">
- **One-sentence behavior statement:** <Who does What, by When — no "and">

sections.heading: Why this one (APEASE + impact rationale)
sections.markdown: <2-4 sentences on the scoring logic that put this above the alternatives>

sections.heading: Candidate shortlist (ranked, not discarded)
sections.markdown:
1. <candidate behavior> — <why it ranked below the selected one>
2. <candidate behavior> — <why it ranked below the selected one>
3. <candidate behavior> — <why it ranked below the selected one>

sections.heading: Open questions / assumptions to check
sections.markdown:
<anything the definer had to guess at from limited program context>
```

sections.heading: Known failure modes
sections.markdown:
- **Compound behaviors slip through.** "Attend antenatal care and adhere to
  iron supplementation" is two behaviors wearing a trench coat. If the
  output statement needs "and" to describe the action, split it before
  passing it downstream — this skill's job is exactly one behavior per run.
- **Outcome dressed up as behavior.** "Reduce anemia" is a health outcome,
  not something anyone *does*. If the selected behavior isn't something a
  specific person could be observed doing at a specific moment, it hasn't
  actually been defined yet.
- **Selecting for measurability over impact.** The easiest behavior to
  observe (e.g. app logins) is sometimes prioritized over the behavior that
  actually drives the goal (e.g. offline saving). APEASE scoring should
  catch this, but only if impact is scored honestly rather than deferred to
  "whatever we can already measure."
- **No real alternatives generated.** If the candidate list is padded with
  strawmen so the preferred behavior wins, the shortlist stops being useful
  as a fallback. Push for candidates that a reasonable person could have
  picked first.
- **Context collapse.** Run on a goal statement with no population or
  setting context, the output's "who" will be generic and the downstream
  diagnosis will inherit that vagueness. Push back to the user for at least
  a rough population and setting before finalizing.
